statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Insufficient facts to determine whether 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires a suspicious activity report here.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that the Secretary require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides related protections (e.g., safe harbor and confidentiality). The fact pattern shows a Singapore-incorporated virtual asset service provider with several very large USD wire transfers labeled “peel-chain hop,” which could be suspicious, but § 5318(g) applicability turns on whether a covered U.S. “financial institution” (as defined/implemented under the BSA and Treasury regulations) was involved and subject to SAR rules, and whether the institution detected facts making the transactions “suspicious” under the applicable SAR standard. The facts do not state (i) that SYN_28f97744 is a U.S.-regulated financial institution or otherwise covered by U.S. SAR regulations, (ii) that the wires were processed through a U.S. financial institution with SAR obligations, or (iii) any specific indicia tying the transactions to a possible violation of law beyond the “peel-chain hop” note. Therefore, it cannot be determined from the provided facts whether § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements are triggered; § 5318(g) requires a suspicious activity report only for covered financial institutions under the implementing rules.
